title: Analysis of an exemplar set work

tips.title: Seven elements, every time
tips.body: Pitch, tonality, structure, sonority, texture, tempo and rhythm, dynamics. The specification lists exactly those seven, and working through them in order means you never stare at a piece wondering what to say. The list does the remembering for you.

tips.title: Structure first, then fill it in
tips.body: Build a **map** of the sections before you analyse anything. Every later observation then has a place to live — *the texture thickens at the chorus*, *it modulates in the middle section*. Analysis without a map is a list of unconnected facts.

tips.title: Every point needs a where
tips.body: A bar number, a section name, a time signature, a chord symbol. **The texture is polyphonic** is an assertion; **the texture is polyphonic from bar 9** is evidence. It costs three words and it is the difference between the middle and the top bands.

tips.title: Analysis explains; description lists
tips.body: A description says what happens. An analysis says what it **does** and **why it is there**. *Brass fanfare* is description. *Brass fanfare, so the opening sounds ceremonial before a note of the tune arrives* is analysis, and only the second earns on both halves of a mark scheme.

steps.title: What you are actually being asked to do
steps.body:
From Year 10 you will study **8 set works**, two in each of the **4 areas of study**.

- **Instrumental Music 1700 to 1820**: Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, third movement; Beethoven: Pathétique sonata, first movement
- **Vocal Music**: Purcell: Music for a While; Queen: Killer Queen
- **Music for Stage and Screen**: Williams: Star Wars main title; Schwartz: Defying Gravity from Wicked
- **Fusions**: Afro Celt Sound System: Release; Esperanza Spalding: Samba em Prelúdio

The written exam is **80 marks**. Section A is **68** and asks questions on **6** of the 8 set works, plus a dictation and an unfamiliar piece. Section B is **12** and compares one set work with an unfamiliar piece.

> 6 of 8 are examined, and **nobody knows which 2 will be left out** until the paper is opened. All 8 have to be known.

That is a lot of music, and the only way to hold it is to learn every piece **the same way**. This topic is that way: a method you apply to each set work in turn, so that by the exam you have 8 analyses built on an identical frame, and comparing any two of them is easy.

The specification organises appraising under three headings:

- **Musical elements**
- **Musical contexts**
- **Musical language**

**Musical elements** is what the music does. **Musical contexts** is why it was written that way — the period, the purpose, the audience. **Musical language** is the vocabulary you use to say both. Nearly all the marks live in the first; the third is how you reach them.

Purcell: Music for a While; Queen: Killer Queen

steps.title: The seven elements
steps.body:
The specification lists **7 musical elements**. Work through them in order and you will never stare at a piece wondering what to say.

**1. Organisation of pitch** — melody and harmony: shape, intervals, chords, cadences.

**2. Tonality** — major, minor, modal, pentatonic, atonal, and any modulations.

**3. Structure** — how the material is organised: the sections, and what returns.

**4. Sonority** — the instruments and voices, and the techniques they use.

**5. Texture** — how the lines fit together: monophony, homophony, polyphony, heterophony.

**6. Tempo, metre and rhythm** — the speed, the grouping of beats, and the rhythmic devices.

**7. Dynamics** — the volume, and how it changes.

Some practical notes on each.

**Pitch.** Is the melody **conjunct** (stepwise) or **disjunct** (leaping)? What is its range? Are there **sequences**, **ostinati** or **riffs**? What chords, and what **cadences** — perfect V to I, imperfect to V, plagal IV to I, interrupted V to VI?

**Tonality.** Not just the key: whether it is **major**, **minor**, **modal**, **pentatonic**, **chromatic** or **atonal**, and where it **modulates**.

**Structure.** Name the form if it has one — binary, ternary, ritornello, ground bass, sonata form, rondo, theme and variations, verse and chorus — and then map the sections with bar numbers.

**Sonority.** Name the instruments and voices, and the **techniques**: pizzicato, tremolo, glissando, harmonics, double stopping, muting, falsetto, melisma, and studio effects.

**Texture.** Count the **lines**, not the players. Monophony, homophony, polyphony, heterophony; also unison, imitation, call and response, continuo.

**Tempo, metre and rhythm.** The speed, the time signature, and the devices: **syncopation**, **dotted rhythms**, **swung rhythms**, **triplets**, **anacrusis**.

**Dynamics.** **Terraced** or **graded**? Where are the loudest and quietest points, and what happens at them?

The two that get forgotten under pressure are **texture** and **dynamics**. Make a point of writing something about each.

steps.title: Build the map before you analyse
steps.body:
The single most useful thing you can do with a new piece is **draw its map**: the sections, in order, with what happens in each.

Do this **before** any detailed analysis, for three reasons.

**Every later point gets a place to live.** *The texture thickens* is a floating fact. *The texture thickens at the chorus, where the three vocal parts enter* is an observation about the piece's shape.

**It reveals the form.** You do not decide a piece is in ternary form and then look for sections; you find the sections and the form names itself.

**It is what the exam gives you anyway.** A question will say *bars 9 to 16* or *the second verse*, and the map is how you find them.

**How to build one.** Play the piece with a pencil and a blank table. For each section write down: where it starts, how long it is, what is playing, and what is new. Four columns is enough.

**What to listen for at the joins.** Sections change at a change of **forces** (someone enters or drops out), a change of **texture**, a change of **key**, a change of **tempo** or **metre**, or a **cadence** followed by something different. Very often several of these happen at once, which is what makes a join audible at all.

**Name the form last.** Once the map exists, the name is usually obvious: two repeated sections is **binary**; A B A is **ternary**; a returning orchestral idea between solos is **ritornello**; a repeating bass is a **ground bass**; verses with a returning chorus is **verse and chorus**; the same music for every stanza is **strophic**.

visuals.alt: An example structure map with four columns recording where each section starts, its length, the forces and what is new

visuals.problem: The map above has four sections. What form is the piece in?

steps.text: Sections 1 and 2 share material; section 3 is different; section 4 is section 1 again.
steps.note: Read the "what is new" column. The shape is in that column, not in the bar numbers.

steps.text: So the shape is A, A varied, B, A.
steps.note: A decorated repeat is still A. Only genuinely new material counts as a new letter.

steps.text: That is ternary form with the opening stated twice.
steps.note: A B A is ternary. The doubled opening is a common way of letting the listener learn the material before it is contrasted.

steps.text: And the modulation at bar 17 confirms it.
steps.note: A contrasting middle section usually moves to a new key. Two independent pieces of evidence agreeing is what an answer needs.

check.prompt: Why should you map the structure of a piece before analysing anything else?
options: The structure carries more marks than any other element
Every later observation then has a place in the piece to belong to
It is the only element that can be heard on a first playing
Examiners always ask about structure before anything else
check.solution: A map turns floating facts into observations about a piece. It also reveals the form rather than requiring you to guess it, and it is how you find *bars 9 to 16* when a question names them. Structure does not carry more marks than the other elements, and several elements are audible immediately.

markScheme.description: so every observation has a place in the piece

steps.title: Context, and the facts you cannot work out
steps.body:
Most of an analysis you can derive from the score and the recording. A small number of things you cannot, and those are the ones to learn.

**For every set work, know:**

- the **composer**, and roughly when they lived
- the **date** of the piece
- the **forces** it is written for
- what it was **written for** — a patron, a play, a film, an album
- which **area of study** it belongs to, and what makes it typical of that area
- one thing about the **composer's other work** or their world

That is six facts a piece, which is manageable. Everything else comes from listening.

**But context only earns when it explains something audible.**

> *Written in 1721* earns almost nothing. *Written for a patron's own players in his own rooms, which is why the ensemble is about twenty strong* earns, because the fact accounts for something you can hear.

That is the test to apply to every contextual sentence you write: **does this explain a feature of the music?** If not, cut it.

**Musical language** is the third heading, and it is the plainest. It means using the right word: *melisma* rather than "a long note on one syllable", *heterophony* rather than "they play it slightly differently", *Tierce de Picardie* rather than "it ends on a major chord". The specification prints a vocabulary list of these terms, and the words on it can be asked about directly.

**Use the tradition's own vocabulary.** *Continuo*, *ground bass* and *word painting* for Purcell; *riff*, *hook* and *double tracking* for Queen; *drone*, *heterophony* and *call and response* for a fusion. Reaching for Baroque vocabulary in a pop song shows you have not placed the extract.

rows: It was written in the Baroque period
A continuo realises the harmony, which places it before about 1750
The composer worked for a wealthy patron
Written for the patron’s own players, which is why the ensemble is small
It comes from a famous musical
The orchestra must leave room for the words, so its textures stay homophonic
The vocal is double tracked, so the sound could not be reproduced live
The cue is 23 bars, because it has to end exactly where the scene does

steps.title: One piece, analysed in full
steps.body:
Here is a complete analysis, built the way every set work should be built: map first, then the 7 elements, then context.

**The piece.** A song for solo voice and small ensemble, described here as an exam would present it.

**Context you are given.** Written in 1732 as part of the incidental music for a play, for the composer's own theatre company: one singer, one cello, one harpsichord.

**On the page.** One flat in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a slow tempo. The words are in English. Bar numbers are printed every four bars, up to bar 40.

**What you hear.**

- Bars 1 to 4: the cello alone plays a four-bar phrase that rises step by step from D and falls back to A at the end of bar 4.
- Bars 5 to 40: that same four-bar phrase repeats nine times without a break, always in the cello, always identical. The harpsichord plays chords above it from bar 5 onwards.
- Bars 5 to 12: the voice enters, one note to each syllable, moving mostly by step within a fifth, quietly.
- Bars 13 to 20: the voice is higher and louder; on the word "rising" it climbs through six notes on that one syllable.
- Bars 21 to 28: the music moves to F major for eight bars, then returns.
- Bars 29 to 36: the voice takes eleven notes over the single syllable "free", the longest note-group in the piece, at the loudest dynamic.
- Bars 37 to 40: the voice sings the bars 5 to 8 material again, quietly, and the final chord is D major rather than D minor.

The working below takes it element by element. Try covering the tables and doing it yourself first.

rows: the cello states its four-bar phrase alone
modulates to F major and back
an eleven-note melisma on "free": the climax
the opening vocal material returns; the last chord is major
props.title: The map, built first

visuals.alt: A structure map of the exemplar piece with six sections, the voice in each and what is new

steps.text: Structure: a ground bass. A four-bar phrase repeats ten times in the cello while the voice above it changes.
steps.note: Stated alone first so the listener learns it, then nine more times. Something fixed with something changing above it.

steps.text: Sonority: solo voice, cello and harpsichord. The cello and harpsichord together form a continuo.
steps.note: A bass instrument plus a chord-playing instrument realising the harmony. Name the combination, not just the instruments.

steps.text: Texture: monophonic for four bars, then homophonic once the voice and harpsichord enter.
steps.note: The cello alone is one line. After that the voice leads and the continuo accompanies, so melody plus accompaniment.

steps.text: Tonality: D minor, modulating to F major at bar 21 and returning; the final chord is D major.
steps.note: F major is the relative major of D minor, so the modulation needs no new accidentals. A minor piece ending on a major chord is a Tierce de Picardie.

steps.text: Pitch: the vocal line is conjunct and within a fifth at first, then wider and higher.
steps.note: The growth of the range across the piece is itself a structural observation, not just a melodic one.

steps.text: Word setting: mostly syllabic, with melismas of six notes on "rising" and eleven on "free".
steps.note: Both are also word painting: the line climbs on "rising", and the longest melisma in the piece lands on "free".

steps.text: Tempo, metre and rhythm: slow, four crotchets in a bar, unchanged throughout.
steps.note: When an element does not change, say so. A fixed tempo under a ground bass is part of why the piece feels relentless.

steps.text: Dynamics: quiet at bar 5, louder at bar 13, loudest at bar 29, quiet again at bar 37.
steps.note: The dynamic shape is an arch, and it peaks exactly where the longest melisma is. Two elements pointing at the same climax.

rows: ground bass: a four-bar phrase, ten times
monophonic for four bars, then homophonic
D minor, to F major at bar 21, Tierce de Picardie at the end
conjunct and narrow, widening across the piece

check.prompt: In that piece, the dynamic peak and the longest melisma both fall in bars 29 to 36. What does that tell you?
options: The composer has made an error, since two effects clash there
Nothing: dynamics and word setting are unrelated elements
Two elements agree on where the climax is, which makes it the climax
It means the ground bass must change at that point too
check.solution: A climax is where several elements arrive together. Here the loudest dynamic and the longest melisma coincide, and neither on its own would be conclusive. Noticing that two independent elements point at the same bar is exactly the kind of observation that separates an analysis from a list — and the ground bass does not change, which is what the climax is happening *against*.

steps.title: Writing it up
steps.body:
An analysis on paper is a sequence of points, and every point has the same three parts.

> **Name the feature. Say where it is. Say what it does.**

*The cello's four-bar phrase repeats ten times from bar 1* — named and located. *...so the music has a fixed frame under a vocal line that never repeats* — what it does. One sentence, two halves, and it earns on both.

**Answer the command word.** Appendix 5 of the specification defines them, and each asks for a different amount.

- **State, give, name, identify, list** — recall or find factual information.
- **Complete** — fill in blanks, for example on a score.
- **Describe** — points, which may or may not be linked.
- **Explain** — points joined to a justification or extension.
- **Compare** — similarities and differences, with relative judgements.
- **Analyse** — examine and dissect musical elements in detail.
- **Evaluate** — judgements against parameters, and conclusions.

The practical consequence: *identify the texture* is a one-word answer, and writing a paragraph on it earns the same one mark while costing you the time you need elsewhere. *Explain* needs the reason attached. *Evaluate* needs you to take a position.

**Length follows the marks.** One mark, one point. Eight marks, eight points or four developed ones. Twelve marks, an argument with a conclusion.

**Do not retell the story.** A set work may have a plot behind it — a Fury being calmed, a witch defying gravity, a rebel ship being chased. The plot is worth a sentence where it explains a musical choice and nothing at all otherwise. The examiner is marking what you heard.

**Use the map when a question names bars.** *Describe the texture in bars 21 to 28* is answerable in seconds if you know what section that is, and a guess otherwise.

points, which may or may not be linked
points joined to a justification or extension
similarities and differences, with relative judgements
examine and dissect musical elements in detail

steps.title: Your turn: analyse it yourself
steps.body:
Here is the exemplar piece again, without the analysis. Work through the 7 elements in order and write one sentence for each. Then check yourself against the table.

**The piece.** A song for solo voice and small ensemble, described here as an exam would present it.

**Context you are given.** Written in 1732 as part of the incidental music for a play, for the composer's own theatre company: one singer, one cello, one harpsichord.

**On the page.** One flat in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a slow tempo. The words are in English. Bar numbers are printed every four bars, up to bar 40.

**What you hear.**

- Bars 1 to 4: the cello alone plays a four-bar phrase that rises step by step from D and falls back to A at the end of bar 4.
- Bars 5 to 40: that same four-bar phrase repeats nine times without a break, always in the cello, always identical. The harpsichord plays chords above it from bar 5 onwards.
- Bars 5 to 12: the voice enters, one note to each syllable, moving mostly by step within a fifth, quietly.
- Bars 13 to 20: the voice is higher and louder; on the word "rising" it climbs through six notes on that one syllable.
- Bars 21 to 28: the music moves to F major for eight bars, then returns.
- Bars 29 to 36: the voice takes eleven notes over the single syllable "free", the longest note-group in the piece, at the loudest dynamic.
- Bars 37 to 40: the voice sings the bars 5 to 8 material again, quietly, and the final chord is D major rather than D minor.

**The discipline.** Write something for **every** element, even where the answer is "it does not change" — that is an observation too, and under a ground bass an unchanging tempo is part of the effect. Locate every point with a bar number. And for at least three of your sentences, add what the feature **does**.

When you have finished, ask yourself the question that separates a description from an analysis: **where is the climax, and how do you know?**

check.prompt: In the exemplar piece the four-bar cello phrase repeats ten times without changing while the voice above it is different each time. Give the two-word term for this structure.
check.solution: A **ground bass**: a repeating phrase in the bass acting as the principal structural element while the parts above it change. The specification describes it as especially Baroque and notably used by Purcell — which, with the continuo and the date, places this piece firmly.

steps.title: Going deeper: analysis rather than description
steps.body:
Everything so far produces a **description**: an accurate account of what happens. A description will reach the middle of a mark scheme and stop. Three things turn it into an **analysis**.

**Say what a feature does.** Not *the texture is homophonic* but *the texture is homophonic, so the words can be followed*. The mark scheme credits an appraising point only where an observation supports it, so a description with no effects attached throws away half the marks available.

**Connect elements to each other.** A description handles the elements one at a time. An analysis notices when they agree. *The dynamic peak and the longest melisma both fall in bars 29 to 36, so that is unambiguously the climax* is a point that neither element could make alone. Composers make climaxes by stacking elements, and noticing the stack is the analysis.

**Say what the piece is an example of.** Every set work is a specimen of something: a Baroque ground-bass song, a Classical sonata-form movement, a fusion, a musical theatre number. Saying what makes it typical — and what makes it unusual — shows you can place it, which is exactly what the unfamiliar question in Section A will ask you to do.

| Description | Analysis |
| --- | --- |
| The bass repeats throughout | The ground ends on chord V, so each repetition resolves only at the next |
| The texture is homophonic | Homophonic, so the words carry; the continuo stays out of their way |
| It modulates at bar 21 | It moves to the relative major, so the shift needs no new accidentals and sounds like light rather than change |
| The last chord is major | A Tierce de Picardie, so a minor piece closes with unexpected brightness |
| There is a melisma on "free" | The longest melisma lands on "free" at the loudest point: word painting and climax together |

The right-hand column is not longer because it says more things. It says the **same** things, and then says why they matter.

boxes.title: Effects, not just features
boxes.body: Every observation followed by what it does. Half the marks live in the second half of the sentence.

boxes.title: Elements agreeing
boxes.body: Notice when two or more peak together. That is how composers build a climax.

boxes.title: What it is an example of
boxes.body: Typical of its area of study in these ways, unusual in these. That is placing the piece.

boxes.title: Evidence everywhere
boxes.body: A bar number on every point. It costs three words and moves you a whole band.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on what turns a description into an analysis

check.prompt: Which sentence is an analysis rather than a description?
options: The four-bar ground bass is repeated ten times during the piece
The piece uses a ground bass, which is a Baroque structural device
The ground bass is played by the cello and the harpsichord together
The ground ends on chord V, so each repetition resolves only at the next
check.solution: It states a feature and then explains the **consequence** — the music can never come to rest. The other three are all accurate and all descriptive: a count, a definition and a list of forces. Each would earn on knowledge; none of them earns on appraisal.

steps.title: The method, in one page
steps.body:
**Before you start.** Learn the six facts you cannot work out: composer, date, forces, what it was written for, which area of study, one thing about the composer's world.

**Then, with the recording:**

1. **Map it.** Sections, bar numbers, forces, what is new. Four columns.
2. **Name the form** from the map, not before it.
3. **Work through the 7 elements in order**: organisation of pitch, tonality, structure, sonority, texture, tempo, metre and rhythm, dynamics.
4. **Locate every point.** A bar number, a section, a chord.
5. **Say what each feature does**, not only what it is.
6. **Look for elements agreeing.** Where two or more peak together, that is the climax.
7. **Say what the piece is an example of**, and where it is unusual.

**When you write:**

- Name the feature, say where it is, say what it does.
- Answer the command word, and write the amount the marks ask for.
- Use the vocabulary of the piece's own tradition.
- Give context only where it explains something audible.
- Do not retell the story.

**And remember why.** 6 of the 8 set works are examined and nobody knows which 2 are left out, so all 8 must be known. 8 analyses built on one frame are far easier to hold than 8 unrelated sets of facts — and when Section B asks you to compare two of them, the frames line up.

one word, justified by the map
what each feature does, not just what it is

questions.solution: Context earns when it **explains something audible**. Who paid for the music accounts for the size of the ensemble you can hear. Reputation, popularity and vague period claims explain nothing about the notes.

options: Structure carries more marks than the other elements do
It is the only element audible on a single first hearing
Every exam question begins by asking about the structure
Later observations then have a place in the piece to belong to
questions.solution: A map turns a floating fact into an observation about the piece: *the texture thickens* becomes *the texture thickens at the chorus*. It also lets the form name itself, and it is how you find the bars a question refers to. Structure carries no more marks than the other elements.

markScheme.description: so every observation has a place in the piece

questions.prompt: Appendix 5 defines the command words. Give the one that means "examine and dissect musical elements in detail".
questions.solution: **Analyse**: the specification defines it as examining and dissecting musical elements in detail, focusing on individual elements and how they combine to create an effect or achieve a purpose. It asks for more than *describe*, which wants only points, and less of a position than *evaluate*.

markScheme.description: analyse

questions.prompt: Which two elements do students most often leave out of an answer?
options: Sonority and tonality
Structure and tempo
Texture and dynamics
Pitch and metre
questions.solution: **Texture** and **dynamics**. The instruments, the tune, the key and the speed all announce themselves; these two have to be noticed deliberately. Both carry marks and both are usually quick to write about, so they are the cheapest marks on the paper to recover.

markScheme.description: texture and dynamics

questions.prompt: A question is worth one mark and begins "Identify the texture in bars 1 to 4." What should you write?
options: A sentence naming the texture and its effect
Two textures, in case the first one is wrong
A short paragraph covering texture and sonority
One word naming the texture
questions.solution: *Identify* is defined as recalling or finding factual information, and the question is worth one mark. One word earns it in full. Everything else earns the same mark while spending time that the longer questions need, and offering two answers means the wrong one may be the one marked.

markScheme.description: one word

questions.prompt: What turns a description of a piece into an analysis of it?
options: Writing about more elements than the question asked for
Saying what each feature does, not only what it is
Using longer sentences and more technical vocabulary
Giving the historical background before the music
questions.solution: A description says what happens; an analysis says what it **achieves**. The mark scheme credits an appraising point only where a musical observation supports it, so a page of accurate description with no effects attached gives away half of what is available.

markScheme.description: say what each feature does

questions.prompt: Give the term for a repeating phrase in the bass that acts as the main structural element while the parts above it change.
questions.solution: A **ground bass**, which the specification calls a repeating phrase in the bass, a type of ostinato, especially found in Baroque music and notably in Purcell. Hearing one answers the structure question and points at the period at the same time.

markScheme.description: ground bass

questions.prompt: Put these steps into the order you should take them when analysing a set work.
items: Map the sections, with bar numbers and what is new in each
Name the form, from what the map shows
Work through the seven musical elements in order
Say what each feature does, not only what it is
Say what the piece is an example of, and where it is unusual
questions.solution: The map comes first because everything else needs somewhere to live. The form follows from the map rather than being guessed before it. The elements come next, since several of them — texture, dynamics, tonality — are described section by section and so need the map. Effects follow the observations that support them. Placing the piece in its area of study comes last, because it is a judgement about the whole and needs the whole to be on the table.

markScheme.description: the map before the form
the elements before their effects
placing the piece in its area of study last

questions.prompt: In a piece, the loudest dynamic and the longest melisma both fall in the same eight bars. What is the significance?
options: Two independent elements agree, so that passage is the climax
The composer has made an error by combining two effects
Nothing: dynamics and word setting are separate elements
It means the structure must change at that point as well
questions.solution: Composers build a climax by **stacking elements**. Either feature alone might be incidental; both arriving together is not. Noticing where elements agree is one of the clearest signs of analysis rather than description, and it is an observation neither element could produce on its own.

markScheme.description: two elements peaking together identify the climax

questions.prompt: Why must all eight set works be learned, when the exam asks about only six?
options: Nobody knows which two will be left out until the paper is opened
The two left out are always from the same area of study
Section B always asks about one of the two that were left out
The unfamiliar listening question is taken from the missing two
questions.solution: 6 of the 8 are examined and the choice is not announced, so 2 go unexamined and there is no way to predict which. Section B uses a set work too, and the unfamiliar piece is by definition **not** a set work, so neither offers a way round it.

markScheme.description: the choice is unknown in advance

questions.prompt: If you learn 7 elements for each of the 8 set works, how many element-by-work observations is that in total?
questions.solution: 7 times 8 is **56**. That sounds like a great deal until you notice that the same 7 questions are being asked every time — which is exactly why one repeatable method beats 8 separate sets of facts, and why comparing any two set works in Section B is straightforward once the frames line up.

markScheme.description: 7 times 8 = 56

questions.prompt:
**The piece.** A song for solo voice and small ensemble, described here as an exam would present it.

**Context you are given.** Written in 1732 as part of the incidental music for a play, for the composer's own theatre company: one singer, one cello, one harpsichord.

**On the page.** One flat in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a slow tempo. The words are in English. Bar numbers are printed every four bars, up to bar 40.

**What you hear.**

- Bars 1 to 4: the cello alone plays a four-bar phrase that rises step by step from D and falls back to A at the end of bar 4.
- Bars 5 to 40: that same four-bar phrase repeats nine times without a break, always in the cello, always identical. The harpsichord plays chords above it from bar 5 onwards.
- Bars 5 to 12: the voice enters, one note to each syllable, moving mostly by step within a fifth, quietly.
- Bars 13 to 20: the voice is higher and louder; on the word "rising" it climbs through six notes on that one syllable.
- Bars 21 to 28: the music moves to F major for eight bars, then returns.
- Bars 29 to 36: the voice takes eleven notes over the single syllable "free", the longest note-group in the piece, at the loudest dynamic.
- Bars 37 to 40: the voice sings the bars 5 to 8 material again, quietly, and the final chord is D major rather than D minor.

Analyse this piece, working through the musical elements and giving a bar reference for each point.
questions.solution:
**Structure.** The cello's four-bar phrase is stated alone in bars 1 to 4 and then repeats **nine more times, identically, to bar 40** — ten statements in all. A repeating bass phrase acting as the structural frame while the parts above it change is a **ground bass**, and stating it alone first is what lets a listener learn it before anything is built over it. Because the frame never moves, every change in the piece is a change in what sits above it.

**Sonority.** One voice, one cello and a harpsichord. The cello plays the bass line and the harpsichord fills in the chords above it from bar 5, so the two together form a **continuo** — the defining accompaniment of Baroque ensemble music, and worth naming as a combination rather than as two instruments.

**Texture.** Bars 1 to 4 are the cello alone: one line, so **monophonic**. From bar 5 the voice leads and the continuo supports, so **homophonic** — melody with subsidiary parts. That is the only textural change in the piece, and it happens at the moment the voice enters.

**Tonality.** The ground rises from D and the piece settles there, so **D minor**. At **bar 21** it moves to **F major** for eight bars and returns — F major is the **relative major** of D minor, so the two share a key signature and the shift needs no new accidentals; the effect is of light rather than of going somewhere else. At **bar 40** the final chord is **D major** rather than D minor: a **Tierce de Picardie**, a minor piece closing with unexpected brightness.

**Pitch and word setting.** The vocal line at bars 5 to 12 is **conjunct**, moving mostly by step, and stays **within a fifth**, so it is narrow and speech-like. Most of the text is **syllabic**, one note to a syllable, which lets the words be followed. Two moments break that. At **bars 13 to 20** the voice climbs through **six notes on the single syllable "rising"** — a **melisma**, and since the line rises on a word meaning to rise, also **word painting**. At **bars 29 to 36** it takes **eleven notes on "free"**, the longest note-group in the piece.

**Tempo, metre and rhythm.** Slow, four crotchets in a bar, **unchanged from first bar to last**. That an element does not change is itself worth stating: an unvarying tempo under an unvarying ground is much of why the piece feels relentless rather than sectional.

**Dynamics.** An **arch**: quiet at bar 5, louder at bar 13, loudest at bar 29, quiet again at bar 37.

**The climax.** The loudest dynamic and the longest melisma both fall in **bars 29 to 36**. Either alone might be incidental; both together make that passage unambiguously the climax, and it happens against a bass that has not altered at all — which is precisely what makes it audible.

**Placing it.** A ground bass, a continuo, extensive word painting and a Tierce de Picardie all point to the **Baroque**, which the given date of 1732 confirms. Written for a play, for a single singer and two players, it is exactly the small-scale theatre music such a company would need.

questions.prompt:
**The piece.** An instrumental movement, described as an exam would present it.

**Context you are given.** Composed in 1805 for a public concert in a large hall, for a full orchestra of about forty players.

**On the page.** Three sharps in the key signature; three crotchets in a bar; a fast tempo; markings including cresc. and dim. Bar numbers printed every eight bars up to bar 64.

**What you hear.**

- Bars 1 to 8: violins play a melody over chords in the lower strings. Four bars, answered by four more that finish the idea. Quiet, and the phrase ends on chord V.
- Bars 9 to 16: the same melody again, now with a flute doubling it an octave higher, and the phrase ends on chord I.
- Bars 17 to 32: new material, louder, with the whole orchestra playing. The music moves to a new key a fifth above.
- Bars 33 to 40: the bars 1 to 8 melody returns in the horns, an octave lower, with every note value doubled.
- Bars 41 to 56: the bars 17 to 32 material again, back in the home key, with a long crescendo.
- Bars 57 to 64: the opening melody once more in the violins, quiet, and a perfect cadence to close.
- There is no harpsichord anywhere in the movement.

Analyse this movement, working through the musical elements and giving a bar reference for each point. Say which period it comes from and why.
questions.solution:
**Structure.** Mapping it first: bars 1 to 8 state a melody (**A**); bars 9 to 16 repeat it with a flute added (**A**); bars 17 to 32 bring new, louder material in a new key (**B**); bars 33 to 40 return the opening in the horns (**A**); bars 41 to 56 bring **B** back in the home key; bars 57 to 64 close with **A** again. So the shape is **A A B A B A** — the opening material returning between contrasting episodes, which is the principle of **rondo**. It is also arch-like, since the movement ends where it began.

**Pitch and phrasing.** Bars 1 to 8 are **four bars answered by four**, like a question and an answer: the first phrase ends on **chord V**, unfinished — an **imperfect cadence** — and at bar 16 the answering phrase ends on **chord I**, finished: a **perfect cadence**. That pairing of an open answer with a closed one is a hallmark of Classical phrasing, and it is only audible because the texture is clear enough not to blur the phrase endings.

**Texture and sonority.** Violins carry the melody over chords in the lower strings from bar 1, so the texture is **melody and accompaniment** — **homophony**. At bar 9 a **flute doubles the melody an octave higher**, which brightens it without adding a new line, so the texture is unchanged and only the colour has moved. At bar 17 the whole orchestra plays. At bar 33 the opening melody is in the **horns an octave lower** with every note value **doubled**, which is **augmentation** — the melody now unfolds at half its former rate although the beat has not changed.

**Tonality.** Three sharps and the music settling there gives **A major**. At bar 17 it moves to the key **a fifth above**, that is the **dominant**, which is the standard destination for a contrasting section in this period, and bars 41 to 56 bring the same material back in the home key. Modulating away and returning is how the movement gets its sense of departure and arrival.

**Tempo, metre and dynamics.** Fast, **three crotchets in a bar**, unchanged. The dynamics are **graded**: the page carries cresc. and dim., and bars 41 to 56 contain a long **crescendo**. Graded dynamics require instruments whose volume responds to touch and to breath, and a body of players who can swell together.

**The period is Classical**, about 1750 to 1820, and the given date of 1805 fits. Three independent reasons agree. There is **no harpsichord anywhere**, so there is no **continuo** — and a continuo is present in almost all Baroque ensemble music, so its absence rules the Baroque out. The texture is **melody and accompaniment** rather than counterpoint, which is the defining Classical change. And the dynamics are **graded rather than terraced**, which a Baroque keyboard could not produce.

**Placing it.** Written for a **public concert in a large hall** for about forty players, which is itself Classical: the music was no longer being made for a patron's rooms, and an orchestra of forty is what a hall and a paying audience needed.

questions.prompt: Which sentence about a set work is an analysis rather than a description?
options: The ground ends on chord V, so each repetition resolves only at the next
The four-bar ground bass is repeated ten times across the piece
A ground bass is a repeating bass phrase, used especially in the Baroque
The ground bass is played by the cello and doubled by the harpsichord
questions.solution: It states a feature and then gives its **consequence** — the music can never come to rest. The others are a count, a definition and a list of forces: all accurate, all descriptive, and none of them explains what the feature achieves.

markScheme.description: the option giving the consequence of the feature

questions.prompt: You have described every element of a set work accurately and given bar numbers throughout. What is still missing for the top band?
options: What each feature achieves, and what the piece is an example of
More elements, beyond the seven the specification lists
The composer’s biography and the circumstances of the first performance
Longer sentences, and a wider range of technical vocabulary
questions.solution: Accurate located description reaches the middle and stops. The top band needs **effects** — what each feature does — and **placing**: what the work is an example of, where it is typical of its area of study and where it is unusual. There are no elements beyond the seven, and biography without an audible consequence earns almost nothing.

markScheme.description: the effects of the features, and placing the work

questions.prompt: A student has learned a set work as a list of facts: the composer, the date, the key, the time signature, the instruments and the names of the sections. Explain why that will not be enough, and describe the method they should use instead.
questions.solution:
**Why a list of facts is not enough.**

**It contains no effects.** Every fact in the student's list is an observation: the key, the metre, the forces, the section names. A mark scheme credits an appraising point only where a musical observation supports it — which means observations are necessary, but on their own they reach the knowledge half of the marks and no further. *The texture is homophonic* earns; *the texture is homophonic, so the words can be followed* earns twice.

**Nothing is located.** An exam question says *bars 9 to 16*, or *the second verse*. A student who knows the piece as a list has no way in: they know the section names but not where the sections are, and they cannot say what is happening at a bar they were asked about. Evidence — a bar number, a chord, a section — is exactly what the level descriptors ask for, and a list has none.

**It cannot be compared.** Section B asks for a comparison between a set work and an unfamiliar piece. A comparison needs the two to be described in the same terms, and a list of facts about one piece has no frame that another piece could be fitted into.

**It will not survive an unexpected question.** 6 of the 8 set works are examined and nobody knows which 2 are omitted. A list prepares for the questions you predicted; a method answers the ones you did not.

**The method instead.**

**Map it first.** Play the recording with a blank table: where each section starts, how long it is, what is playing, what is new. Four columns. Everything else will hang off this.

**Name the form from the map.** Not before it. Once the sections are written down, *binary*, *ternary*, *rondo*, *ground bass*, *verse and chorus* usually names itself, and you have the evidence for the name in front of you.

**Work through the 7 elements in order**: organisation of pitch, tonality, structure, sonority, texture, tempo, metre and rhythm, dynamics. One sentence each, and write something even where the answer is that an element does not change, because that is an observation too. Texture and dynamics are the two most often forgotten.

**Locate every point.** A bar number costs three words and moves an answer a whole band.

**Add the effect.** For every feature, what does it do? That is the half of each sentence the student's list is missing entirely.

**Then place the piece.** What is it an example of? What makes it typical of its area of study, and where is it unusual? This is what lets you recognise the unfamiliar extract in Section A, which is chosen precisely because it resembles a set work.

**Why one method beats eight lists.** Learning 8 pieces in the same 7 categories means 56 observations arranged in a grid rather than 8 unrelated heaps. Anything you know about one piece has a slot in every other, which makes revision cumulative instead of repetitive — and when Section B asks you to compare two of them, the frames already line up, so the comparison writes itself.

examTechnique.body:
**What this topic is for.** In Year 10 and Year 11 you will study **8 set works**, two in each of the **4 areas of study**. The exam asks about **6** of them, and nobody knows which 6 until the paper is opened, so all 8 have to be known. This topic is the method you will use on every one.

**Work through the 7 elements in order.** Organisation of pitch, Tonality, Structure, Sonority, Texture, Tempo, metre and rhythm, Dynamics. The list is the specification's own, and following it means never running out of things to say.

**Map the structure first.** Sections, bar numbers, what returns. Everything else hangs off it.

**Locate every point.** A bar number, a section, a chord. Evidence is what the level descriptors ask for.

**Name the feature, then say what it does.** Both halves, in that order. An appraising point is credited only where a musical observation supports it.

**Learn the facts that cannot be worked out.** Composer, date, forces, the circumstances it was written in. Everything else you can derive from the score and the recording; those you cannot.

**Answer the command word.** *Identify* wants a word; *describe* wants points; *explain* wants points joined to reasons; *compare* wants similarities, differences and a judgement; *evaluate* wants a conclusion.

**Know how it sits in its area of study.** Every set work is an example of something, and the unfamiliar extract in Section A will be chosen to resemble one of them.
examinerErrors: Describing what happens without ever saying what it achieves.
Making points with no bar number, section name or other location.
Retelling the story or the background instead of describing the music.
Working through some elements and forgetting others: dynamics and texture are the ones most often dropped.
Learning a set work as a list of facts rather than as a piece with a shape.
Using the vocabulary of the wrong tradition for the piece in front of you.
Giving context that explains nothing audible — a date on its own earns almost nothing.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer has a map of the piece in its head before it writes anything, so every observation has a place. It works through the 7 elements without having to be prompted, and it locates every point in the score. It always says what a feature does as well as what it is, and it knows which of the two the command word is asking for. It uses the vocabulary of the piece's own tradition, and it can say what the work is an example of — what makes it Baroque, or a fusion, or musical theatre — rather than treating it as an isolated object.
